criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community rural drinking water service access (piped house connections and public standpipes) in Hai and Siha districts, Tanzania.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines formal and informal institutional, administrative, and governance arrangements in decentralized rural water supply (Community Based Management via a legally established Water Service Facility Trust, seven autonomous Water Trusts, and Village Water Committees). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes — explicitly analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access, connection, billing, enforcement, and accommodation, including: (1) tariff, metering, and full-cost private connection rules (standardized metered billing, structured full-cost-recovery tariffs, and full upfront payment by applicants for private yard connections vs. public standpipes for those unable to afford house connections); (2) utility ownership/regulatory structure (legally established WSFT, constitutionally autonomous Water Trusts insulated from local government interference, and formal annual performance appraisals with constitutional sanctions and fines); and (3) formal and informal enforcement and accommodation mechanisms governing payment and continued access (disconnection enforcement vs. village water committee cross-payment to prevent standpipe disconnection, public naming/shaming of bill defaulters in churches/mosques, and informal means-testing/accommodation by local churches liaising with tap attendants to pay bills for needy households). Both plain and narrow readings support inclusion.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal/institutional empirical case study based on fieldwork in 2012–2016 and late 2017, comprising 20 purposively/snowball-sampled semi-structured interviews in Kiswahili with bureaucrats, politicians, water trust/WSFT officials, and village and religious leaders, alongside operational and appraisal records. Qualitative empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports rural drinking water service outcomes including access coverage (92% of ~366,696 population served via 25,043 piped connections and 1,682 public taps), continuity/reliability (24/7 supply for household connections and scheduled daytime supply at public standpipes), affordability, revenue collection, and avoidance of standpipe disconnection.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (Water Service Facility Trust, 7 Water Trusts, Village Water Committees, and served rural communities/households in Hai and Siha districts, Tanzania; n = 20 key-informant interviews), exposure (formal billing/tariff/connection/autonomy/appraisal rules interacting with informal enforcement sanctions and payment-accommodation norms), outcome (drinking water access, connection type, continuity, affordability, and disconnection avoidance), and study design (qualitative institutional case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (field interviews conducted in Kiswahili and analysed/reported in English by the authors).

evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper, we examine a case of superior rural water access in two Tanzanian districts, where actors not only acknowledge, but actively harness informality to provide access to water to rural populations.

Our data consists in interviews (conducted in Kiswahili) with several actors in the rural water sector—bureaucrats, politicians, village and religious leaders. We collected data in two phases: between 2012 and 2016 during the execution of a large interdisciplinary research program and in late 2017.

Supply of water on a 24/7 basis is true only for house connections. Public standpipes do not supply water at night, because the water seller is not available at night. However, all citizens are aware of when to expect water at public standpipes.
Applicants for private connections pay full costs for private connections from the main pipeline or branch pipeline to the household yard.
The professional management of the trusts is reinforced by the WTs’ full autonomy from the government system of human resource management.

As part of its outreach programme to the less fortunate, the Lutheran church pays some water bills of its members, if it can be assured that they cannot afford to pay them themselves, liaising with the tap attendants.
However, if the water attendant (who is a member of a water committee) fails to pay the water bills, the water committee members pay the bill themselves to avoid shame

raw_response.exposure: Formal institutional and regulatory water-service rules (legally established Water Service Facility Trust and constitutionally autonomous Water Trusts, standardized metered billing, structured full-cost-recovery tariffs, upfront full-cost private yard connection rules, and annual performance appraisals with sanctions/fines) complemented by informal rules, enforcement sanctions, and accommodation practices (public naming/shaming of non-payers in churches/mosques, church means-assessed bill subsidies coordinated with tap attendants, diaspora financing of household connections, and Village Water Committee solidarity payments to prevent public tap disconnection)
raw_response.outcome: Rural drinking water service access (92% coverage; 25,043 piped customer connections and 1,682 public standpipes), continuity/reliability (24/7 household supply and timetabled daytime standpipe supply), affordability, revenue collection/cost recovery, and avoidance of standpipe disconnection
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural water governance organizations (Water Service Facility Trust, 7 Water Trusts, and Village Water Committees serving ~366,696 residents) and rural communities in Hai and Siha districts, Kilimanjaro region, Tanzania; qualitative sample of 20 purposively/snowball-selected actors (bureaucrats, politicians, water officials, village and religious leaders) interviewed across two fieldwork phases (2012–2016 and late 2017)
raw_response.rationale: This full-text qualitative empirical case study in Hai and Siha districts, Tanzania satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Using semi-structured interviews (n = 20) and organizational fieldwork data, it examines how formal rule-type mechanisms governing rural drinking water access—including autonomous Water Trust legal structures under a Water Service Facility Trust, structured cost-recovery tariffs, metered billing, full-cost private connection fee rules, disconnection threats, and performance-appraisal sanctions—interact with informal enforcement sanctions (naming/shaming non-payers) and informal accommodation/cross-subsidy mechanisms (means-assessed church bill support with tap attendants, diaspora connection funding, and committee arrears payment to avert public tap disconnection) to shape household piped connections, public standpipe access, 24/7 continuity, and affordability. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking quantitative effect sizes.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative institutional case study (semi-structured key-informant interviews and fieldwork/organizational document analysis)
